title: A Differentiated Suburban Landscape: Socioeconomic Variation Across Detroit’s Inner- and Outer-Ring Suburbs
content: This study examines neighborhood socioeconomic differences across the tri-county Detroit metropolitan area, focusing on patterns between its inner- and outer-ring suburbs, and the city of Detroit between 2010 and 2023. Using the Modified Darden–Kamel Composite Socioeconomic Index (CSI), a multidimensional measure of neighborhood socioeconomic status, places are classified into low-, middle-, and high-CSI categories. The analysis describes patterns of racial and ethnic composition, immigrant settlement, and household structure across this socioeconomic hierarchy, drawing on the spatial assimilation and place stratification perspectives. The results reveal a socioeconomic hierarchy, with outer-ring suburbs at the highest positions, inner-ring suburbs mostly in intermediate positions, and Detroit at the lower end. Moreover, both suburban rings are internally differentiated, with varying socioeconomic conditions within each. Racial and ethnic composition, immigrant settlement, and household structure also vary across CSI categories and suburban rings. These patterns remained largely stable between 2010 and 2023, although socioeconomic and demographic shifts occurred within each category. Overall, the findings show that suburban areas in the Detroit metro area are not homogeneous. Differentiating between inner- and outer-ring suburbs reveals important differences in neighborhood socioeconomic conditions.
